title: Pistons’ talks with Jalen Duren, Ausar Thompson ‘haven’t been’ progressing just yet
content:
DETROIT — Jalen Duren will be a restricted free agent this summer, while Ausar Thompson is eligible for a rookie-scale extension that would begin in the 2027-28 season. Both will likely be expensive and are Detroit Pistons franchise pillars alongside Cade Cunningham on a team that led the Eastern Conference with 60 regular-season wins.

Trajan Langdon, Detroit’s president of basketball operations, spoke in May about how the Pistons will look to retain both Duren, an All-NBA Third Team member, and Thompson, who was named to the All-Defensive First Team. When asked Thursday how negotiations have been progressing, however, Langdon said, “They haven’t been” just yet.

“Those will be conversations that will be had. But to be completely honest, you will never know how those conversations go,” Langdon said.

Before those conversations really kick into high gear, the Pistons will have the 21st pick in next week’s NBA Draft. Though Langdon mentioned the possibility of moving up in the draft, he expressed confidence in Detroit’s ability to find a quality player if it stays put.

“For us, it will be, who’s the best player there,” Langdon said when asked if he’ll target a 3-point shooter or playmaker. “It will be, does that player fit this environment? Does he fit our identity? How can that player help us? Maybe it’s not even next year, but in the future, right? We have players that are going to get expensive. We’re going to have to have our picks hit and be able to help our team.

“So maybe it’s not a player that helps us next year per se but can help us throughout the course of his career after that.”

Apart from the draft, Thompson and Duren, Langdon reiterated Detroit will continue to “be very thoughtful and intentional” in how it goes about looking to acquire talent, whether that be on the trade market or through free agency, which begins June 30.

“That’s the tricky part, is trying to balance everything, trying to find things that fit,” Langdon said. “If it’s a trade, then it has to be a trade that we feel is worthwhile. We’re not going to go out and give out too many assets for a player. … Not having those assets down the road (can) hamper us in terms of making another move.

“We’re having internal thoughts and talks every day right now, the closer we get to that time.”

Langdon said the team is in the midst of a week of voluntary workouts during which 10 or 11 players returned to Detroit for offseason work before any mandatory offseason workouts begin. He added that he believes the “best way” for Detroit to grow will be internally taking a step forward, though the Pistons will explore all options externally as well.

While many Pistons fans seem to hold out hope for his return, one external addition who remains unlikely is Malik Beasley. The 29-year-old guard last played in the NBA during Detroit’s 2025 playoff run before a federal gambling investigation derailed his NBA career. Beasley played professionally in Puerto Rico last season with the Santurce Crabbers.

“No, I have not,” Langdon said when asked if he’s been in communication with Beasley. “He doesn’t have an agent right now, either. So that would make it hard.”

Langdon seems intent on building on last season’s success. But what exactly does success look like for a Detroit team that was a win away from reaching the Eastern Conference finals?

“You’ve got to win the second round for us to be better,” Langdon said. “It doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve got to win 64 games. I don’t think we’re trying to do that. If we do, that’d be fantastic. We know that we need to be more equipped to compete in the postseason. That’s what we’re looking at doing, again … adding pieces that help accentuate our three best players, our core three players.

“That will help us not only in the regular season, but in postseason play as well. I think that all goes into (how) we feel we need to get better.”

As for championship contention next season?

“What we like to do is talk about championship habits, championship environment, championship approach,” Langdon said. “A lot of things have to go right to win it. … I don’t gauge my success on if we win a championship or not, or our success every year, because you can have a great year — I think we had a great year — did we come up short? Yes, at the end of the day. Did we have a successful season? Absolutely.”
